one_liner: C#/.NET AVX2 and AVX-512 array math (Exp, Ln, Sin, Erf, normal CDF, Sqrt), 5-7x over a scalar System.Math loop.
what_it_does: A .NET library (NuGet package Kolbe.LitMath, 0.7.0) of vectorised elementary functions: Exp, Ln/Log2, Sin, Cos, Tan, ATan, Erf, normal-distribution CDF, Sqrt, polynomials, dot products and branch-free helpers (Max, Min, IfElse). The array API is Lit.Exp(in Span<double> x, ref Span<double> y) (or an allocating overload returning a new Span), and every function also has Vector256<double>/Vector512<double> overloads so several functions can be chained in registers in one pass over the data. It replaces element-by-element System.Math calls, not a vector math library API such as MKL VML.
how_it_is_fast: Hand-written System.Runtime.Intrinsics code processes 4 doubles per AVX2 vector, or 8 per AVX-512 vector when running on .NET 8 with AVX512F, with the span loop unrolled four times. Exp computes 2^(x*log2 e) by rounding to the nearest integer n, evaluating a degree-11 polynomial in FMA (split odd/even Horner chains) on the fraction, and building 2^n from exponent bits (AVX2) or VSCALEFPD (AVX-512). Ln extracts exponent and mantissa (bit masks on AVX2, VGETEXPPD/VGETMANTPD on AVX-512) and evaluates a fitted series of the atanh form ln(d) = 2*atanh((d-1)/(d+1)), with one division per vector.
when_to_use: C# or F# code on x86-64 servers with AVX2 and FMA (or AVX-512 under .NET 8) that applies Exp or Ln to arrays of doubles or floats: 5.2-7.3x over a System.Math loop in the author's AVX-512 table, 2.4-3.3x on AVX2 in the older table.

Small and medium arrays (a few to about 2,000 elements) where P/Invoke marshalling into Intel MKL dominates: the author's older table has LitMath ahead of MKL.NET Vml.Exp by 4.5x at 3 elements, 1.6x at 64 and 1.3x at 2,048.
Composite element-wise formulas (option pricing, normal CDF, Erf) written once against the Vector256 overloads so the array is traversed a single time instead of once per function.
Workloads whose Exp arguments stay small in magnitude (roughly |x| < 30), where the Exp polynomial is within a few ulps.
when_not_to_use: Large arrays where you can call MKL: in the author's own older table MKL.NET Vml.Exp was 4.3x faster at 65,536 elements and 2.0x faster at 32,000,000.

Non-x86 or pre-AVX2 hardware: apart from the AVX512F switch there are no IsSupported checks or scalar fallbacks, so ARM64 (including Apple silicon) and CPUs without AVX2/FMA get PlatformNotSupportedException.

Code that needs correct edge cases or full double accuracy at large magnitudes: Ln(0) returns +Infinity on the AVX2 path, Exp error grows to about 220 ulps near |x| = 700, and the AVX-512 paths have the bugs listed under gotchas.
Projects that need maintenance: the last commit was 2024-03-28 (README edits), there are no issues or releases on GitHub, and the README calls the AVX-512 numbers preliminary.
C or C++ code: this is a managed .NET library.

integration.form: shared lib (NuGet package Kolbe.LitMath, a managed .NET assembly; source is a small set of C# files)
integration.dependencies: none beyond the .NET runtime (System.Runtime.Intrinsics); benchmarks use BenchmarkDotNet 0.13.1, MathNet.Numerics 5.0.0 and MKL.NET 1.3.2 (win-x64)
integration.min_toolchain: .NET 6 for the AVX2 paths; .NET 8 for the AVX-512 paths (multi-targets net6.0 and net8.0)
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 and FMA required; AVX-512F used automatically on .NET 8; no ARM64 or scalar fallback
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the functions are static and keep no shared mutable state apart from static readonly constant vectors, so concurrent calls on disjoint spans look safe (code reading)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same math as System.Math.Exp/Log, but called on spans or Vector256/Vector512 values rather than per scalar, and results differ in the last bits and at edge cases

gotchas: Correctness bugs in the AVX-512 paths (found by reading the code; emulated in Python with the repo's constants, not run on AVX-512 hardware): Two(Vector512) picks the polynomial's integer part with RoundScale (round to nearest even) but scales by VSCALEFPD of x + 0.5, which floors, so when x*log2(e) is exactly 0.5, 2.5, -1.5 and similar ties the result is doubled, e.g. Exp(0.5*ln 2) gives 2.828 instead of 1.414. Ln(Span<double>) with 5 to 7 elements takes a 4-lane Vector256 masked path while VSZ is 8, so outputs 4 to n-1 are never written; the allocating Ln(in Span<double>) overload then returns uninitialised memory there. The AVX-512 Ln also drops the NaN/zero/infinity masking of the AVX2 path. The tests cover n = 1, 3, 9, 15, 33, 62 and negatives only at n = 4 (which takes the AVX2 path), so none of this is caught.
Ln(0) returns +Infinity on the AVX2 path, because Constants.Double.Log.NEGATIVE_INFINITY is created from double.PositiveInfinity (same typo in the Vector512 constant block).

Exp reduces with a single multiply by log2(e) and no Cody-Waite split, so the error grows with |x|: about 1.6 ulps on [-1, 1], 14 ulps up to |x| = 30 and about 220 ulps near |x| = 600-700 (emulated); the README's 'Exp at double precision limits' only holds near zero. Ln has about 3.6e-15 absolute error but relative error up to roughly 1e-12 (AVX2) to 2e-11 (AVX-512) just below 1.0 from cancellation.

Harness and example flaws: the README points to LitExpDoubleParallel as the way to go multicore, but it slices Slice(i, n) instead of Slice(i*n, n), so the tasks overwrite overlapping copies of the first N/cores elements and most of the array is never computed. In the timed benchmarks the naive loops store into one scalar field while LitMath writes an output array, LogBenchmark at N = 64 is Log(1.0) for every element (integer division), ExpBenchmark feeds Exp(Log(k)) for integers k = 0..100, and the committed ExpBenchmark runs only N = 3,200,000, not the published 64 and 100,000. Span tails reprocess the last vector with overlap, so calling a function in place (same span for input and output) applies it twice to some tail elements when n is not a multiple of the vector width.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LitMath only from .NET code on x86-64; for C++ the Vector Class Library or corvus give vectorised exp/log/sin in-process, and math_intrinsics and SIMD-math-prims cover single-precision approximations in C. Among .NET siblings, SimpleSIMD and LinqFaster vectorise reductions and LINQ operators, not transcendental functions.
verified_claims_summary: A BenchmarkDotNet table in the README, from an unnamed AVX-512 machine on an unstated runtime (AVX-512 needs .NET 8), times a scalar loop of System.Math.Exp/Log (calling the platform C runtime's exp/log) against Lit.Exp/Lit.Ln on 64 and 100,000 doubles: Exp 218.69 vs 42.34 ns and 354,492 vs 64,728 ns (5.2x and 5.5x), Log 137.06 vs 24.89 ns and 259,986 vs 35,793 ns (5.5x and 7.3x). The benchmark inputs (no exact ties, no zeros, lengths that are multiples of 8) avoid the bugs above, so the timings stand but say nothing about edge-case correctness.
status_note: Stale since 2024-03-28 (last code change 2023-12; 79 stars, no GitHub issues), Apache-2.0 and published on NuGet as Kolbe.LitMath 0.7.0. Usable for AVX2 double Exp and Ln in .NET if you avoid zero inputs, in-place calls and the AVX-512 paths until the rounding, short-span and special-value bugs are fixed.
